text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Tuesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

-Swedish banking shares have risen 40 percent since the beginning of 1996, compared with an overall bourse rise of 30 percent, as foreigners as well as Swedish investors calculate that the shares are undervalued. The banking index rose 3.5 percent on Monday alone, helped by renewed speculation that S-E-Banken may seek to buy the state's residual stake in Nordbanken.

-Kinnevik's television companies TV3, TV 1000 and ZTV continue to lose money, according to the company's nine-month results. Although the company dominated by businessman Jan Stenbeck showed a nine-month profit of 247 million crowns compared with 409 million, only a one-time income from shares in Netcom prevented the whole group from plunging into the red.

-Investor AB reiterated when announcing nine-month results that it was seeking a partner for its wholly-owned Saab AB subsidiary, whose profit fell to 84 million crowns from 223 million one year ago. The two main problems were falling financial income because of lower interest rates, and continued losses in the production of civilian aircraft.

-Swedish Railways (SJ) director general Stig Larsson confirmed that the system must shed 1,500 jobs to reduce its losses calculated at an annual 500 to 700 million crowns. But unions say 38 percent of jobs have already been lost between 1988 and 1995 and further cuts are not the answer.

-The Nature Protection Agency wants to scrap the present system of classifying the environmental effects of cars and introduce a new system which would favour vehicles with low carbon dioxide emissions, more effective exhaust filters and engine-warming devices. But the EU would have to approve any new regulations first.

-The opposition Conservatives are considering seeking a vote of no-confidence in Prime Minister Goran Persson unless he explains remarks which appeared to give comfort to China's hard-line handling of dissent. Persson is expected to make a statement in the foreign policy council on Wednesday.

-More than one in four Swedes, totalling 2.4 million people, has a cellular telephone. Sales this year are estimated at one million phones and a further 1.1 million next year, according to the MTL association of phone suppliers. Sweden's Ericsson and Nokia of Finland are the largest suppliers.

-The world's largest solar power installation begins operations this week in Denmark. The 8,000 square metre field, equivalent to five football pitches, has been equipped on the island of Aeroe where the sun shines 10 percent longer than in the rest of Denmark.

-Scandinavian Mining AB, a gold and precious metals prospecting company, said it will list its stock on the SBI exchange and issue new shares for 45 million crowns. The company, founded in 1992, is drilling at four places in northern Sweden. Its stock will be sold in blocks of 500 at 20 crowns per share.
